title: Populations and communities
summary: How ecologists estimate population size, why populations follow sigmoid growth up to a carrying capacity, and how species in a community interact through competition, predation, mutualism and chemical inhibition.

keyterms.definition: A group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time, which can interbreed.
All the populations of different species living and interacting in an ecosystem.
Estimating population size of sessile organisms by counting them in randomly placed quadrats and scaling the mean density up to the whole area.
Estimate of population size from capture-mark-release-recapture: (number first captured and marked × number in second sample) ÷ number of marked individuals recaptured.
The maximum population size of a species that an environment can sustainably support, limited by competition for resources.
A factor, such as competition, predation or infectious disease, whose effect increases as population density rises, giving negative feedback control.
S-shaped population growth curve with exponential, transitional and plateau phases.
An interaction between members of the same species, which may be competition or cooperation.
An interspecific relationship in which both species benefit, e.g. root nodules in Fabaceae, mycorrhizae in Orchidaceae, zooxanthellae in hard corals.
An interspecific relationship in which one organism (the parasite) lives on or in a host, benefiting at the host's expense.
A non-native species that spreads rapidly in a new ecosystem, often out-competing endemic species for resources.
A statistical test comparing observed with expected frequencies; used to test for association between two species in quadrat samples.
Top-down: populations limited by predators or herbivores at a higher trophic level. Bottom-up: limited by availability of nutrients or producers.
Release of chemicals by a plant into the environment that inhibit the growth of nearby plants of other species.

questions.prompt: Which is the best definition of a population?
options: All the organisms in an ecosystem
Organisms of different species that interact in an area
All members of a species worldwide
A group of organisms of the same species living and interbreeding in the same area
questions.explanation: A population is one species in one area. All interacting species together form a community.

questions.statement: Random quadrat sampling is suitable for estimating populations of sessile organisms.
questions.explanation: Sessile organisms (e.g. plants, barnacles) stay in place, so they can be counted in quadrats. Motile animals would move in or out and are estimated by capture-mark-release-recapture.

questions.prompt: 40 beetles were caught and marked. Later, 50 were caught, of which 10 were marked. Estimate the population size.
questions.explanation: Lincoln index = (40 × 50) ÷ 10 = 200. One in five recaptured beetles was marked, so the 40 marked beetles are about one fifth of the population.

questions.text: Lincoln index: population size = (number first marked × number in second sample) ÷ number of marked individuals ___.
questions.explanation: The proportion of marked individuals in the second sample is assumed to equal the proportion of marked individuals in the whole population.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of capture-mark-release-recapture in order.
items: Capture a sample of animals and count them
Release them and allow time to mix with the population
Capture a second sample and count marked and unmarked animals
questions.explanation: Marked animals must mix randomly back into the population before resampling, otherwise the proportion recaptured will not represent the whole population.

questions.statement: Quadrats should be placed where the organisms are most common to give an accurate estimate.
questions.explanation: Quadrats must be placed randomly (e.g. using random-number coordinates) to avoid bias; choosing dense patches would overestimate the population.

questions.prompt: The mean number of plants per 1 m² quadrat is 3.5. The field is 200 m². Estimate the population size.
questions.explanation: Population = mean density × total area = 3.5 m⁻² × 200 m² = 700.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: All interacting species in an area
Able to move from place to place

questions.explanation: Sessile organisms are sampled with quadrats and motile organisms with capture-mark-release-recapture; populations of many species together make a community.

questions.text: Organisms that do not move, such as plants or barnacles, are described as ___.
questions.explanation: Sessile organisms stay in one place, so random quadrat sampling gives a reliable estimate of their population density.

questions.prompt: Some marks rub off animals between capture and recapture. How does this affect the Lincoln index estimate?
options: It has no effect
It underestimates the population
It overestimates the population
It makes the estimate exactly correct
questions.explanation: Fewer marked animals are recognised in the second sample, so the denominator is too small and the estimate is too large.

options: The maximum population size an environment can sustainably support
The maximum rate of population growth
The number of offspring an individual can produce
The population size at the start of the exponential phase
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is set by limited resources such as food, water, space or light; competition for these resources prevents further growth.

questions.prompt: Put the phases of a sigmoid population growth curve in order.
questions.explanation: Growth is exponential while resources are plentiful, slows in the transitional phase as limiting factors increase, and levels off at carrying capacity.

questions.statement: During the exponential phase, resources are plentiful and limiting factors have little effect.
questions.explanation: With abundant resources and few density-dependent effects, birth rate far exceeds death rate and the population grows exponentially.

options: A volcanic eruption
A severe frost
Infectious disease
A flood
questions.explanation: Infectious disease spreads more easily in dense populations, so its effect increases with density. Natural disasters affect populations regardless of density.

questions.text: The maximum population size an environment can sustainably support is the ___ capacity.
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is reached when competition for limited resources makes birth rate equal to death rate.

questions.prompt: Why is control by density-dependent factors an example of negative feedback?
options: It always causes the population to go extinct
It makes the population grow faster as it gets larger
It acts only on small populations
As density rises, these factors increase death rate or reduce birth rate, returning the population towards carrying capacity
questions.explanation: The larger the population, the stronger the effect of competition, predation and disease, which counteracts the change and stabilises population size.

questions.statement: In the plateau phase, the birth rate is much greater than the death rate.
questions.explanation: In the plateau phase the population is at carrying capacity, so birth rate (plus immigration) roughly equals death rate (plus emigration).

questions.prompt: Match each phase of the sigmoid curve to its description.

pairs.right: Birth rate greatly exceeds death rate
Growth slows as resources become limiting
Birth rate about equals death rate

questions.explanation: The changing balance of birth and death rates, driven by competition for resources, produces the S-shaped curve.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of cooperation within a species?
options: Two oak trees competing for light
Wolves hunting together in a pack
A fox eating a rabbit
Mistletoe growing on a tree
questions.explanation: Intraspecific relationships include both competition (e.g. for light or mates) and cooperation (e.g. pack hunting). Foxes and rabbits, and mistletoe and trees, are different species.

questions.text: Sigmoid growth can be modelled by counting the fronds of ___ growing in a container of water over several weeks.
questions.explanation: Duckweed (or yeast) reproduces quickly in a limited space, so the full exponential, transitional and plateau phases can be observed in a short time.

options: A group of organisms of one species
The non-living parts of an ecosystem
All the interacting populations of different species in an ecosystem
A food chain
questions.explanation: A community includes every population of every species in an area, along with their interactions.

questions.prompt: Match each interspecific relationship to its description.

pairs.right: One lives on or in a host, harming it
One animal kills and eats another
An animal feeds on a plant
Two species use the same limited resource

questions.explanation: These categories describe how one species affects another in a community; pathogenicity is another category, where a pathogen causes disease in its host.

questions.prompt: How do Rhizobium bacteria and plants of the Fabaceae (legume family) both benefit from root nodules?
options: The bacteria photosynthesise for the plant
The plant digests the bacteria for protein
The bacteria provide carbon compounds; the plant provides nitrogen
The bacteria fix nitrogen for the plant; the plant supplies the bacteria with carbohydrates
questions.explanation: This mutualism lets legumes grow in nitrogen-poor soils, while the bacteria receive energy-rich carbon compounds and a protected environment.

questions.statement: In hard corals, zooxanthellae photosynthesise and supply the coral with carbon compounds, while the coral provides shelter and nutrients.
questions.explanation: This is mutualism. When stressed, corals expel zooxanthellae (bleaching) and may starve.

questions.text: Orchids (Orchidaceae) rely on ___ fungi in their roots to supply nutrients, especially as seedlings.
questions.explanation: Mycorrhizal fungi absorb minerals from the soil for the orchid and, in return, can receive carbon compounds once the orchid photosynthesises.

questions.prompt: Why can invasive species out-compete endemic species?
options: They are always larger than endemic species
They often lack natural predators and diseases in the new area, so their populations grow rapidly
They cannot reproduce in the new area
They only eat food that endemic species do not use
questions.explanation: Without their usual density-dependent controls, invasive species can take resources that endemic species need, reducing endemic populations.

questions.prompt: A chi-squared test for association between two plant species gives χ² = 6.2. The critical value (1 degree of freedom, p = 0.05) is 3.84. What should be concluded?
options: Reject the null hypothesis: there is a significant association between the species
Accept the null hypothesis: the species are distributed independently
The species must be mutualistic
The test is invalid
questions.explanation: Because χ² is greater than the critical value, the difference between observed and expected frequencies is significant. The test shows association (positive or negative), not its cause.

questions.statement: Top-down control means a population is limited mainly by the availability of nutrients or producers.
questions.explanation: That is bottom-up control. Top-down control is limitation by predators or herbivores at a higher trophic level.

questions.prompt: Put the events of a predator–prey cycle in order, starting with an increase in prey.
items: More food is available, so the predator population increases
Increased predation reduces the prey population
Less food is available, so the predator population falls
Reduced predation allows the prey population to recover
questions.explanation: Predation is density-dependent control: predator numbers track prey numbers with a time lag, producing linked oscillations.

questions.text: The release of chemicals by a plant that inhibit the growth of nearby plants is called ___.
questions.explanation: Allelopathy reduces competition from other plants. Similarly, some fungi and bacteria secrete antibiotics to inhibit competing microorganisms.
